title: BAR U1·W3 — Business Combinations & Consolidated Financial Statements (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — when one company controls another

BAR's technical-accounting area tests the hard consolidations the core sections only introduce. When MBG acquires a specialty subcontractor to bring electrical work in-house, accounting must combine two companies into one set of statements under the acquisition method, recognize goodwill, carve out the noncontrolling interest, and eliminate everything the two entities did with each other. This week builds that consolidation.

The acquisition method (ASC 805)

Every business combination uses the acquisition method. The acquirer (1) identifies itself and the acquisition date, (2) recognizes the acquiree's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value — even ones the target never booked, like internally developed intangibles — and (3) recognizes goodwill or a bargain-purchase gain. Acquisition-related costs (legal, advisory) are expensed as incurred, not capitalized — a favorite exam point. Contingent consideration (an earnout) is recorded at fair value on the acquisition date.

Goodwill and the bargain purchase

Goodwill is the residual: consideration transferred + the fair value of any noncontrolling interest + the fair value of any previously held equity interest, minus the fair value of the net identifiable assets acquired. Worked example: MBG pays $800,000 for 80% of the sub, the 20% NCI fair value is $200,000, and the target's net identifiable assets have a fair value of $900,000. Goodwill = ($800,000 + $200,000) − $900,000 = $100,000. If instead the fair value of net assets exceeded the total consideration, the acquirer would recognize a bargain-purchase gain in earnings after rechecking its measurements.

The noncontrolling interest

When the parent buys less than 100%, the noncontrolling interest (NCI) — the outside owners' share — is reported within consolidated equity, not as a liability, and is measured at fair value at acquisition (the full-goodwill approach US GAAP uses). On the consolidated income statement, net income is shown in total and then allocated between the controlling interest and the NCI. The NCI rises with its share of subsidiary income and falls with its share of dividends — the same mechanics as the equity method, but presented inside the consolidated equity section.

The consolidation process

Consolidation combines the parent and subsidiary line by line and then eliminates the double-counting. The core eliminations: remove the parent's investment-in-subsidiary account against the subsidiary's equity (replacing it with the fair-valued assets and goodwill); eliminate intercompany receivables and payables; eliminate intercompany dividends; and eliminate intercompany sales and the related cost of sales. Without these, the consolidated statements would overstate assets, revenue, and equity by counting internal transactions as if they were with outsiders.

Eliminating intercompany profit

The subtle elimination is unrealized intercompany profit. If the acquired electrical sub sells materials to MBG at a markup and MBG has not yet used them on a job, the profit on that inventory is not yet earned from the group's perspective and must be deferred until the goods are sold outside the group. The same applies to intercompany sales of equipment (deferring the gain and adjusting depreciation). For downstream sales (parent to sub) the deferral reduces the controlling interest; for upstream sales (sub to parent) it is shared between the controlling interest and the NCI in proportion to ownership.

Goodwill impairment and VIEs

Goodwill is not amortized by public companies; it is tested for impairment at least annually at the reporting-unit level, writing it down when the unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value (a private company may elect to amortize goodwill instead). Consolidation is also required when control exists without majority ownership: a variable interest entity (VIE) is consolidated by its primary beneficiary — the party with the power to direct the activities that most affect the VIE's performance and the obligation to absorb its losses or right to receive its benefits. The VIE model exists precisely to stop off-balance-sheet structuring of controlled entities.

Reading the consolidated result

The payoff of all this machinery is a single set of statements that presents the parent and its controlled subsidiaries as one economic entity, with outside owners shown as NCI and internal transactions erased. For an analyst applying last week's ratios, this matters enormously: a consolidated balance sheet shows the group's true leverage and the goodwill that a string of acquisitions has piled up, while the intercompany eliminations ensure the revenue and margins reflect only real, outside business. Combinations done well build capacity; combinations that generate mostly goodwill and intercompany churn are a warning the ratios will eventually expose.

The measurement period and step acquisitions

Two timing rules round out the acquisition method. The measurement period gives the acquirer up to one year to finalize provisional fair values as new information about acquisition-date facts emerges, with adjustments applied retrospectively to goodwill rather than to current earnings. A step acquisition — gaining control over a previously held equity interest — requires remeasuring that prior interest to fair value at the acquisition date, with the resulting gain or loss in earnings, before computing goodwill. This is why the goodwill formula includes the fair value of any previously held interest: control is treated as a fresh start that re-bases the whole investment.

Intra-entity debt and the consolidation worksheet

When one member of the group holds the other's bonds, consolidation treats the debt as retired from the group's perspective: the intercompany payable and receivable are eliminated, and any difference between the carrying amounts (a constructive gain or loss on extinguishment) is recognized in the consolidated statements. More broadly, the consolidation worksheet is where it all comes together — the parent and subsidiary trial balances are combined, the elimination entries are posted in worksheet columns (never on either company's books), and the consolidated totals fall out. Mastering which entries are worksheet-only versus recorded on the legal entities is exactly what the BAR consolidation simulations test, and the eliminations repeat every period the intercompany relationship persists, because the worksheet starts fresh from the legal-entity books each time.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 1 distinguished significant influence (equity method) from control (consolidation); BAR completes the picture with the full acquisition method, NCI at fair value, and the intercompany eliminations. The intercompany-elimination logic is the same discipline as the CMA construction-group consolidations across MBG's related entities.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the acquisition method: identifiable assets/liabilities at fair value; expense acquisition costs.
  2. Compute goodwill = consideration + NCI fair value + prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets; recognize a bargain-purchase gain if negative.
  3. Present NCI at fair value within consolidated equity; allocate consolidated net income to controlling and noncontrolling interests.
  4. Eliminate intercompany balances, sales, dividends, and unrealized profit; test goodwill for impairment; consolidate VIEs by their primary beneficiary.

Recap: the acquisition method fair-values the acquiree and books goodwill as the residual (MBG's purchase yields $100,000 of goodwill), NCI sits in consolidated equity at fair value, and consolidation eliminates intercompany balances, sales, dividends, and unrealized profit; goodwill is impairment-tested (not amortized) for public companies, and a VIE is consolidated by the primary beneficiary that controls it; the measurement period allows up to a year to finalize fair values, a step acquisition remeasures any prior interest to fair value before goodwill, and intra-entity bonds are treated as retired on consolidation — all of it posted on the consolidation worksheet, not the legal-entity books, and repeated each period the relationship persists.

flashcards.back: Recognize the acquiree's identifiable assets/liabilities at fair value; EXPENSE acquisition-related costs; record contingent consideration at fair value.
Consideration transferred + NCI fair value + fair value of any prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets acquired.
When fair value of net assets exceeds total consideration; recognize a gain in earnings after rechecking measurements.
Outside owners' share, measured at fair value at acquisition and reported within consolidated equity (not a liability).
Eliminate investment-in-sub against sub equity, intercompany receivables/payables, intercompany dividends, and intercompany sales/COGS.
Defer profit on intercompany sales until the goods/assets leave the group; upstream deferrals are shared with the NCI.
Public-company goodwill is tested for impairment, not amortized; a VIE is consolidated by its primary beneficiary (control + absorbs losses/benefits).

questions.q: Under the acquisition method, acquisition-related costs (legal, advisory) are:
questions.explain: ASC 805 requires acquisition-related costs to be expensed, not capitalized.

questions.q: Goodwill in a business combination equals:
choices: Consideration + NCI fair value + prior interest − fair value of net identifiable assets
Purchase price − book value of net assets
questions.explain: Goodwill is the residual after fair-valuing net identifiable assets and including NCI and any prior interest.

questions.q: MBG pays $800,000 for 80%, NCI fair value is $200,000, and net identifiable assets are $900,000. Goodwill is:

choices: Within consolidated equity at fair value
questions.explain: US GAAP presents NCI within consolidated equity, measured at fair value at acquisition.

questions.q: Unrealized profit on an intercompany sale of inventory still held by the buyer is:
choices: Deferred until the goods are sold outside the group
questions.explain: Intercompany profit is not earned by the group until the goods leave it, so it is deferred.
Public-company goodwill is impairment-tested at least annually; private companies may elect to amortize.

questions.q: A variable interest entity (VIE) is consolidated by:
questions.explain: The primary beneficiary — the party that controls the VIE and absorbs its losses/benefits — consolidates it.
